title: Exact certificate-size bounds and a linear-resolution benchmark for the finite truth-table checker
claim: For the accepted finite truth-table row-certificate semantics, every accepted certificate has at least 2^n rows and the minimum is exactly 2^n for every unsatisfiable input. The all-falsified-row generator has exactly the sum of 2^(n-d_j) over non-tautological indexed clauses, where d_j counts distinct variables. A minimally unsatisfiable n-variable implication chain has n+1 clauses, minimum row-certificate size 2^n, generator size (n+3)2^(n-2) for n>=2, and an explicit n-step resolution refutation. This is a supported nonformal note with reproducible finite checks, not a Lean theorem or complexity-class separation.
novelty: Known elementary counting and resolution methods, integrated with the precise artifacts accepted in PRs #19 and #14. PR #19 already warns that enumeration is exponential, but does not give a tight optimum for every accepted certificate, the clause-sensitive exact generator count, or a minimally UNSAT comparison family and reproducible edge-case data. The contribution is a quantitative specification and regression benchmark, not a new proof-system lower-bound technique.

prior_art.relationship: Primary object of analysis: its exact check and certificate definitions. It already discloses exponential enumeration; this note quantifies the lower bound and exact generator size without claiming its completeness result as new.

Accepted list-based resolution checker supplies the comparison semantics. The note explains the n-step trace on an implication chain without importing a formal theorem or claiming a machine-checked representation conversion.

Classical proof-complexity context distinguishing proof length and relative proof-system efficiency. The public abstract was inspected; the specific elementary counting application is derived in the note and is not claimed as a new general lower-bound method.

research_direction: Proof complexity: exact certificate sizes, finite UNSAT baselines, and separating benchmarks
